Usually, a good source is daily papers, reviews or gig guides. Bob Vylan and Joe and the Shitboys are two of my favourite bands that I found by reading what was going on at some playground in north London. [And] I have sources – a couple people in New York; someone in LA, another DJ; a couple people in Paris – that send me things. At first, I did everything with vinyl and a legal pad. It got harder and harder, and then someone much younger explained to me how to use Spotify, so I use that as a tool. A really good source is reading the posters from festivals, because some of them will have 30, 40, 50 artists and groups, most of whom you've never heard of. If you just save an image of it and go down the list, you'll find some really good stuff.

I try to have a clear slate. I call it "sneaking up on the song". You've got a track you like, and maybe you don't have an idea. You're listening to the track, and you give it a little time when you just feel really good. And maybe something comes out – bang! – and you know it right away, and you're very excited. Give it 15 minutes, give it an hour, and then drop it before it becomes work. You will have to work it up later, but don't let it become work when you're creating it. For many people, including myself, the whole song gets done in that one burst. But sometimes it takes two or three bursts. Sometimes you have a burst and then [the] second burst doesn't come until four or five years later.
